top_choice_rationale: P001 (B002, Kiyotaki and Moore) is my first choice on achievement, maturity, attribution and citation scope. Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is an original general-equilibrium mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and credit, so temporary shocks become persistent and amplified. It has almost three decades of use in macro-finance, quantitative macro and policy modelling. The founding paper has two authors, so the credit is the cleanest on the slate and the citation can be tightly bounded. I judge the mechanism distinct from the 2022 prize on banks, runs and intermediation. Adjacency to a recent prize is a balance consideration, not a merit criterion. Direct identification of the size of collateral amplification is weaker than the theory's influence, and I cannot quantify it from the supplied record, so this stays a discount on my choice. P002 (B012, Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn) is second. Its demand-estimation core has stayed standard through three decades of critique, and the citation is worded narrowly. Its weaknesses are the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, and a toolkit that rests on structural assumptions. P000 (no award) is last because both proposals describe mature, defensible achievements.
recusal_note: I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and an IIES colleague of both. Both support P001, so their agreement is not independent confirmation of merit. My profile shows no apparent connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn. My long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow concerns a candidate who is not on this slate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
